note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — TWO RACEMES, THEN ROOTED RUNNERS
tiles.details: Begin with TWO full one-sided V-shaped racemes in gallery panel 2 (index 1). Check the wetland mat in panel 6 (index 5) and the actually rooted green RHIZOME in panel 1 (index 0): two separate nodes carry visible roots on a horizontal underground stem. This is NOT an aboveground stolon at the soil surface; that required photo is still missing. Bahiagrass at gallery panel 7 (index 6) ALSO has a convincing paired V, so never certify from raceme count alone.
tiles.short: Usually two one-sided racemes forming a V; confirm a creeping stolon rooted at an actual node.
tiles.status: REAL V-SHAPED HEAD + ROOTED RHIZOME — SURFACE STOLON STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · COLLAR AND TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
tiles.details: TWO physically archived Harry Rose originals show the clear translucent true membranous ligule emerging from the inner blade/sheath mouth: gallery panels 3 and 8 (indices 2 and 7). The newly installed photo is a separate higher-resolution 1600x1200 angle (Flickr/Commons photo 8250242625), with an existing visual-only gross arrow to the actual membrane, NOT the sheath hairs. Both photos lack a physical mm ruler; 0.5–1.5 mm is the original photographer's stated range, not an independent measurement from these JPEGs. Other floras give different ranges, so confirm in the field.
tiles.short: Expose the inner blade–sheath junction; published ligule lengths vary by flora.
tiles.status: TWO AUTHENTIC TRUE LIGULE MACROS ARCHIVED — PHYSICAL MM MEASUREMENT STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · RIPE SPIKELET ROWS AND REDUCED LOWER GLUME
tiles.details: Panel 4 (index 3) shows authentic aligned narrow green spikelets on a flowering raceme, distinct from one entire raceme. To confirm the 2.4–4 mm published range, photograph five mature spikelets with a 1-mm bar; lower glume may be reduced or absent and upper glume needs a real dissected view. No microscopic lemma/glume arrows are approved from the unscaled image.
tiles.short: Measure five mature flat-convex spikelets, generally about 2.4–4 mm long.

tiles.heading: 04 · STERILE VERSUS FERTILE LEMMAS; NO LONG AWN
tiles.details: The existing source-authenticated panel 4 (index 3) is a whole attached spikelet close-up, NOT a photo of the upper/lower lemmas separately. At 10–20× expose a lower sterile and hardened upper fertile floret, locate lower/upper glume and palea, and place a 1-mm ruler in the SAME plane. Dangling anthers and feathery stigmas in the head photo are not awns.
tiles.short: One lower sterile floret and one upper fertile floret; hardened upper lemma is awnless.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED REPRODUCTIVE KEY — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTED FLORETS

tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — BAHIA, THIN PASPALUM, DALLISGRASS
tiles.details: The final gallery panel 7 (index 6) is a REAL separately labelled *Paspalum notatum* head with the same V shape as panel 2 (index 1). Gallery panel 5 (index 4) is *Paspalum setaceum*, not knotgrass. To distinguish, physically trace the surface runners and roots, then compare mature spikelets and ligule. Panel 1 (index 0) only documents underground rhizome, not bahiagrass rootstock or knotgrass stolon. Dallisgrass also has a different, generally more robust many-raceme habit, but no matching Dallisgrass photo is displayed here.
tiles.short: Never call knotgrass from the two-raceme V alone.
tiles.status: BOTH BAHIA AND THIN PASPALUM PHOTO COMPARISONS COVERED — ROOTSTOCK COMPARISON OPEN

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — EXACT TWO-LANE HANDOFF
tiles.details: EIGHT GALLERY PANELS: six same-species actual locally archived knotgrass JPEGs (rooted underground rhizome, V-shaped paired flowering head, TWO true ligule anatomical angles, elliptic attached spikelet closeup and wetland mat) plus other-species *P. setaceum* and *P. notatum* comparisons. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a SAME verified Texas individual with true soil-surface aboveground STOLON visibly rooting at its node and attached full head, plus physical mm bar on one true ligule and a mature spikelet dissection (upper glume, lower sterile lemma, hardened upper fertile lemma). NEEDS_SITE_QA: photograph licenses, separate-source identifications, eight gallery panels, original annotation endpoints, live public Pages and mobile readability. Do not infer Hays BONAP from Australian photos.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — six own-species archived photographs, one local bahiagrass file, and one shared thin-paspalum photo.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: KNOTGRASS / WETLAND PASPALUM: the two narrow unilateral V-shaped flowering racemes are a first clue only (bahiagrass can look the same). Follow the creeping wetland mat to ACTUAL nodes: gallery already shows an authentic root-bearing RHIZOME, true short inner membranous ligule, attached flowering racemes and oval spikelets. An aboveground root-bearing STOLON at a visible soil line and calibrated glume/lemma series remain missing; do not use the rhizome photo as a substitute.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Panel 1 (index 0): roots emerge from multiple nodes on a photographed underground creeping RHIZOME with attached shoot. This is clear evidence of real roots, NOT an aboveground rooting stolon at a visible soil line.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: TWO physically archived Harry Rose originals show the clear translucent true membranous ligule emerging from the inner blade/sheath mouth: gallery panels 3 and 8 (indices 2 and 7). The newly installed photo is a separate higher-resolution 1600x1200 angle (Flickr/Commons photo 8250242625), with an existing visual-only gross arrow to the actual membrane, NOT the sheath hairs. Both photos lack a physical mm ruler; 0.5–1.5 mm is the original photographer's stated range, not an independent measurement from these JPEGs. Other floras give different ranges, so confirm in the field.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Begin with TWO full one-sided V-shaped racemes in gallery panel 2 (index 1). Check the wetland mat in panel 6 (index 5) and the actually rooted green RHIZOME in panel 1 (index 0): two separate nodes carry visible roots on a horizontal underground stem. This is NOT an aboveground stolon at the soil surface; that required photo is still missing. Bahiagrass at gallery panel 7 (index 6) ALSO has a convincing paired V, so never certify from raceme count alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Search actual growing horizontal stems and root-bearing nodes, rather than interpreting two racemes alone. Bahia grass P. notatum also often makes two racemes; grass-root habit and mature upper-glume/spikelet measurements must corroborate. The Australian wetland image is not proof of Texas nativity.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: Harry Rose's specimen shows a continuous green horizontal rhizome or creeping basal stem, with branching fibrous roots descending from two regions and a fresh green shoot rising near the right-hand root mass. This is real underground vegetative spread, NOT a photo showing a surface stolon rooted into undisturbed moist soil. Root bases are visible; same-individual flowering architecture is not.

These are visible flowering structures, not dissected glumes/lemmas. No root-bearing stolon or scale is shown.

intro: KNOTGRASS / WETLAND PASPALUM: the two narrow unilateral V-shaped flowering racemes are a first clue only (bahiagrass can look the same). Follow the creeping wetland mat to ACTUAL nodes: gallery already shows an authentic root-bearing RHIZOME, true short inner membranous ligule, attached flowering racemes and oval spikelets. An aboveground root-bearing STOLON at a visible soil line and calibrated glume/lemma series remain missing; do not use the rhizome photo as a substitute.
memory_rule: COUNT COMPLETE RACEMES → MEASURE 5 RIPE SPIKELETS → CHECK MARGINAL HAIRS → ROOTED BASE/COLLAR. DALLIS few large silky; VASEY many small silky; FLORIDA few big round; PUBIFLORUM smaller oval; SETACEUM narrow variable; DISTICHUM two + real stolons.
safety_note: Eight visible gallery panels: SIX true knotgrass photos, TWO other-species comparisons; seven physically stored files in this species images folder (six own, one P. notatum), plus separately archived P. setaceum in its own folder. True underground rhizome, two genuine inner ligule angles and paired inflorescence covered; actual visible soil-rooting ABOVEGROUND stolon and mature dissected glumes/lemmas still absent. Public Pages deployment unverified.
field_rule: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Search actual growing horizontal stems and root-bearing nodes, rather than interpreting two racemes alone. Bahia grass P. notatum also often makes two racemes; grass-root habit and mature upper-glume/spikelet measurements must corroborate. The Australian wetland image is not proof of Texas nativity.
